0.note: The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

1.q: רָצִ֣יתָ יְהוָ֣ה אַרְצֶ֑⁠ךָ שַׁ֝֗בְתָּ שבות יַעֲקֹֽב
1.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [You showed favor to your land, Yahweh, by restoring the captivity of your people] or [You favored your land, Yahweh; indeed, you restored the captivity of Jacob]

The psalmist is using the name of a man, **Jacob**, to refer to his descendants. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the name of the people instead. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

2.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [You completely forgave all the sins of your people]

The psalmist is speaking of forgiving sin as if that were to physically carry the burden of the ones who sinned. If your language does not have a comparable expression, or if this image does not communicate well, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You forgave the iniquity of your people]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to mean that **your people** committed **the iniquity**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the idea behind the possessive form with a verb or in some other way. Alternate translation: [the wickedness that your people did]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **the iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what your people did wrong]

The psalmist is speaking of forgiving sin as if it were covering something so that it could no longer be seen. If your language does not have a comparable expression, or if this image does not communicate well, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you forgave all of their sin]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **their sin**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what they did sinfully]

3.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [You completely stopped being angry with us]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **your wrath**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how wrathful you were]
Meaning fierce anger, **the burning of your nose** was a common expression. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your fierce anger]

4.note: The psalmist is using the imperative form to make a request to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a form that is more natural for a request. Alternate translation: [Please restore us, God of our salvation]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **God** as characterized by **salvation**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the idea behind the possessive form in another way. Alternate translation: [God who saves us]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [saving us]

The psalmist is using the imperative form to make a request to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a form that is more natural for a request. Alternate translation: [and please break up your vexation with us]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **your vexation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how vexed you are]

5.note: The psalmist is using the question form to express a plea. If you would not use the question form for this function in your language, you could translate this as a statement or an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Please do not be angry with us forever.]

The psalmist is using the question form to express a plea. If you would not use the question form for this function in your language, you could translate this as a statement or an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Please do not prolong your anger to every generation.]

The psalmist is using the word **nose** to represent anger, since a person’s nose may flare or become hot when angry. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the name of the emotion instead. Alternate translation: [your anger]

The expression **to generation and generation** was a common expression meaning “for a long time into the future.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for all future generations]

6.note: The psalmist is using the question form to express a plea. If you would not use the question form for this function in your language, you could translate this as a statement or an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Please return to us.]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb form translated as **will you not return** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he is posing the question to Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, will you not return]

The psalmist is using a jussive form to express a wish directed to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a form that is more natural for a request. Alternate translation: [Please revive us]

The psalmist has been speaking to God using the pronoun **us**, referring to himself and the people together, but now he switches to the third person, saying **your people**. The psalmist is referring to the same group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could maintain the same person throughout. Alternate translation: [we, your people]

7.note: The psalmist is using the imperative form to make a request to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a form that is more natural for a request. Alternate translation: [Please make us see your covenant faithfulness]

The psalmist is speaking of experiencing God’s covenant faithfulness as if it were something that could be physically seen. If your language does not have a comparable expression, or if this image does not communicate well, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Make us experience your covenant faithfulness, Yahweh]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **your covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how faithful you are to your covenant with us]

The psalmist is using the imperative form to make a request to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a form that is more natural for a request. Alternate translation: [and please give your salvation to us]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **your salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and give your saving help to us]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to mean that both **covenant faithfulness** and **salvation** come from God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the idea behind the possessive form in another way. Alternate translation: [the covenant faithfulness that you show, Yahweh, and the salvation that you give us]

8.note: Up to this point, the psalmist has been speaking on behalf of the community, using **us** and **we**. Now the psalmist shifts to speaking individually, saying **me**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could clarify this. Alternate translation: [Let me, the psalmist, hear]

In this verse, the result is stated before the reason. The psalmist wants to hear what God will speak, and the reason is that God will speak **peace** to his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could reverse the order and put the reason before the result. Alternate translation: [because he will speak peace]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [peaceful things]

The psalmist is saying what he wants **his people** to do. See the discussion in the introduction to Psalms about this form of speech and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [but they should not return to folly]

The pronoun **them** refers to the people and faithful ones mentioned earlier in the verse. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the referent more explicitly. Alternate translation: [but let his people not return]

The psalmist is speaking of resuming a sinful way of life as if it were physically turning around and going back to a place. If your language does not have a comparable expression, or if this image does not communicate well, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but let them not begin acting foolishly again]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **folly**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to foolish behavior]

9.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **his salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [his saving help]

The psalmist is using the adjective **reverent** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [to the people who revere him]

The psalmist is using the word **for** to introduce the purpose for which God’s salvation is near. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make the purpose relationship more explicit. Alternate translation: [so that glory may dwell in our land]

The psalmist is using the word **glory** to represent God’s manifest presence among his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state this meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for God’s glorious presence to dwell in our land]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [glorious presence]

9.q: אַ֤ךְ ׀ קָר֣וֹב לִ⁠ירֵאָ֣י⁠ו יִשְׁע֑⁠וֹ לִ⁠שְׁכֹּ֖ן כָּב֣וֹד בְּ⁠אַרְצֵֽ⁠נוּ
9.note: In this verse, both uses of the pronoun **his** refer to Yahweh, and the pronoun **our** refers to the psalmist and the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could clarify the referents. Alternate translation: [Surely Yahweh’s salvation is near to the people who revere Yahweh, for glory to dwell in the land of the people of Israel]

10.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [God will be completely faithful, true, righteous, and peaceful toward his people]

The psalmist speaks of **Covenant faithfulness** and **truth** as if they were people who could **meet together**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God will be both faithful to his covenant and true to his word at the same time]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **Covenant faithfulness** and **truth**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [Being faithful to his covenant and being true to his word]

The psalmist speaks of **righteousness** and **peace** as if they were people who could **kiss** in greeting. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [doing what is right and having peace will go together]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **righteousness** and **peace**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [acting rightly and being at peace]

11.note: The psalmist speaks of **Truth** as if it were a plant that could **sprout from the earth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Faithfulness will flourish among people on earth]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **Truth**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Truthful communication]

The psalmist speaks of **righteousness** as if it were a person who could **look down from the heavens**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the right actions of God will descend from the heavens]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and just actions]

12.note: The psalmist speaks of **our land** as if it were a person who could **give** something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and our land will yield its produce]

13.note: The psalmist speaks of **Righteousness** as if it were a person who could **walk** ahead of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will act rightly in all he does] or [Righteousness accompanies all that Yahweh does]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **Righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [What is right]

13.q: צֶ֭דֶק לְ⁠פָנָ֣י⁠ו יְהַלֵּ֑ךְ וְ⁠יָשֵׂ֖ם לְ⁠דֶ֣רֶךְ פְּעָמָֽי⁠ו
13.note: The pronouns **him** and **his** refer to Yahweh. The pronoun **it** refers to righteousness. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the referent more explicitly. Alternate translation: [Righteousness walks before Yahweh, and righteousness puts Yahweh’s steps in the way]
